summary.en: The Kinks and the Who were two distinctive forces within the British Invasion.
summary.zh: The Kinks和the Who，是英伦入侵潮流中的两支独特力量。

body.zh:
说到the Beatles类或者the Rolling Stones类的乐队，有两支乐队真的不能简单划分到这任意一种当中。他们就是the Kinks和the Who。在我们谈及的这一时期，也即64年到66年里，他们都在英国取得了很大的成功。其实the Kinks在美国也取得了一些成绩，但the Who遭到的冷遇就令人吃惊了，只有几首歌在这个国家成为了长期热门的单曲。好，我就不过早讲述这些事情了，以免打乱安排。

The Kinks和the Who之所以难以归类，一大原因是他们都以强有力的、富有侵略性的音乐闻名。这让他们看起来有点像the Rolling Stones，我是说那种来自布鲁斯音乐的影响，那种力量感和那种由吉他主导的演奏。而且，在强有力的音乐之外，两支乐队都展现出了自己的智慧。他们创作的歌词饱含思量，体现了一种接近于真正的歌曲作者的写作手法。这说来又更接近the Beatles也即John Lennon-Paul McCartney二人组了，倒不太像Mick Jagger和Keith Richards。所以说，the Kinks和the Who融合了两大乐队的风格。乐队的主创，无论是the Kinks的Ray Davies还是the Who的Pete Townshend，都突出表现了强有力的音乐手法、糅合了两大乐队的特征，从而创造出他们自己的风格，难以被简单划分为the Beatles类乐队或the Stones类乐队。

如我之前所讲，这两个乐队都没有像the Beatles或the Stones那样在美国闹出巨大动静。The Kinks在单曲上取得了更多成绩，但在收获辉煌成功的路上遇到了一点小麻烦，因为他们不知怎地搞得被美国禁止入境了。我想，大概是他们的举止太过狂放，导致移民局的人不愿意再次发放签证。由于不能重访美国、亲身推广自己的音乐，他们在唱片销售上有些举步维艰。The Who则一直没取得多大成功，直到1967年单曲《I Can See For Miles》登上了榜单第9位才算是小有成就。他们真正在美国取得成功的起点是《Tommy》，而这就不在本章的讨论范围内了。我们会在讨论迷幻音乐的时候提到它，发表于1969年的《Tommy》。

一说到the Kinks的作品，我就想到了像《You Really Got Me》这样的歌曲。它在1964年登上过英国榜单的第1位和美国榜单的第7位。非常硬朗、富有侵略性的曲子，开场是一段吉他lick，其可能稍微受到了《Louie Louie》的影响。70年代末，Van Halen翻唱过《You Really Got Me》。《All Day And All of The Night》——如果你也会弹吉他，它在你眼中和《You Really Got Me》是非常相似的。你会发现，只需稍微改动弹奏《You Really Got Me》时用到的指法，就可以用之于弹奏《All Day and All of The Night》了。这就是我们从匠人视角看到的东西。乐队发现这种手法在《You Really Got Me》中收效不错，于是对其略作修改，凭借《All Day And All Of the Night》带来了几乎相同的东西。这种事情在流行乐产业里十分常见。第一首歌，《You Really Got Me》，在英国榜单登顶了。第二首则登上榜单第2位。这两首都是热门单曲。1964年，第二首歌同样在美国得到了第7名的成绩。歌曲《Tired Of Waiting For You》 也用到了与《You Really Got Me》、《All Day And All Of the Night》类似的和弦走向，不过这次乐队采用了琶音演奏（arpeggiate）的手法，歌曲间的相似因而不太明显。这首歌在1965年登上了英国榜单的第1位和美国榜单的第6位。歌曲《Till the End Of the Day》沿用了上述歌曲中的特点，它在1965年获得了英国榜单的第6名，但没有登上美国排行榜。Ray Davies本打算继续如此创作，但John Lennon的歌词开始包含更多哲学意味，Dylan也在1965夏天成为了一位重要的表演者，于是Davies的歌词随之变得更具哲学性，开始反思社会、表达对现状的不满。歌曲《A Well Respected Man》是个好例子，他在其中批评了从众的现象和庸常的期望，人们都带着伪装，从不展露自己的真实性格；他们应当表现真我、真诚待人。这种批判的成分，你可以从Bob Dylan的《Ballad of A Thin Man》或John Lennon的《Nowhere Man》中看到；这下就还要加上Ray Davies了。

现在让我们把注意力转向the Who。从多个方面讲，这支乐队都是有趣人物的集合体。Pete Townshend，乐队的吉他手，一位杰出的歌曲作者，他负责为乐队创作歌曲和提出总体的概念。但他只负责部分演唱，也即唱唱和声、时而领唱一段。演唱主要由Roger Daltrey负责。他有点类似Robert Plant随后在60年代末和70年代扮演的角色，也即那种性感的主唱，纯粹负责演唱曲调。从很多方面来看，还有点像是Mick Jagger或Elvis Presley那样的人物。还有名为Keith Moon的狂野鼓手和名为John Entwistle的老练贝斯手。置身这四人之中，你会听到带有人声的强力三重奏，其释放的音乐强而有力，背后还有愈发复杂的歌词和概念。谈及the Who，我们首先会想起的热门单曲就是《My Generation》。1965年，这首歌在英国登上了排行榜第2位，但很多人都会感到惊讶的是，同年它并未在美国流行起来。事实上，这首歌从未打入美国的榜单。我们常常觉得它曾做到了，是因为the Who在70年代取得了巨大成功，以至于乐队那些60年代初的单曲被拿到广播上不停播放。如今它们也进入了经典摇滚广播歌曲之列，所以看似它们本来就是热门单曲。但《My Generation》在当时并非如此。不仅是它，《I Can't Explain》，这另一首我们常听到的曲子，65年在英国取得了第8名，但同样未在美国成为热门单曲。《Substitute》，1965年发表的又一首重要歌曲，在英国取得了第2名，在美国却没有水花。如我之前所说，《I Can See For Miles》是一项突破，但那已经是1967年的事情了。前面也提到，乐队的大突破是1969年的《Tommy》。

The Who还是英国发生的某场运动的一部分。这场运动几乎与美国无关，它叫做“The Mods”。若看过电影《Quadrophenia》，你应该会对此有所了解。Sting也参演了这部电影。它很有趣，可以说是对the Who的概念专辑《Quadrophenia》的一种电影式阐释。故事背景设定在布莱顿海滩，那儿有两拨价值观不同的年轻人掀起了一场著名的骚动。The Rockers是那种身穿皮衣、梳着油亮背头的人们，带着链子、骑着大哈雷摩托。The Mods则是那种发型整齐，干净卫生的人，他们不骑大摩托而喜欢骑Vespa小踏板车，颇有点花花公子的味道。某个周末，这两拨人终于在布莱顿海滩碰面并掀起了一场决斗。这是一场牵涉整个城市的骚动，报纸上全是Mods与Rockers对垒的事情。最终，the Who成了Mods运动所选择的代表性乐队。美国并未真正发生过一场Mods运动，但当时的Mods人群喜欢听Motown公司发行的唱片，经常跳舞，the Who几乎是他们的偶像乐队。他们是Mod文化的一部分。在英国，这种Mod与Rocker相对立的情况，也见诸the Beatles的电影《A Hard Days Night》。片中某处，乐队成员遭遇了一连串的发问。有人问John Lennon，你是怎么发现美国的？Lennon说，在格陵兰左转。又有人问Ringo，你是个Mod还是个Rocker？这指的就是布莱顿海滩事件。他回答说，都不是，我是个Mocker。当然，在1964年的美国，没人明白他们说的是些什么。不过这听起来很有趣，而对英国人来说，但凡对当时的流行文化有所了解，都会立马明白个中意思。那么，the Who是与the Mods有紧密联系的乐队，这种联系也多少助推了乐队在英国榜单上取得好名次。但由于美国没有发生Mod运动，他们的音乐未能真正打入美国。

好，至此我们已经讲过the Kinks和the Who了。是时候回顾一下，在这一整章的课程里，我们都讲到了哪些内容。事实证明，英伦入侵为英国艺人开启了新的机遇。不仅是英国本土，对美国而言，这些新面孔的出现同样震动了美国的音乐产业。事实上，我们也曾目睹过类似情况。1955年到1957年，那些来自独立厂牌的唱片，一时间都往主流流行乐榜单跨界。它们反而令主流厂牌的唱片变得边缘化了。于是主流厂牌连忙赶制类似的唱片。人们对业内发生这种事情感到惊讶，而我们也能看到事情是怎样收场的。贿赂丑闻在1959年、1960年频频发生，业界巨头再次掌握了话语权。1964年初，类似的情况在美国再度上演。The Beatles等一批英国艺人来到这里，取得了巨大成功。这是一种新的威胁，所以常见的叙事是，英伦入侵彻底震动了美国的音乐产业，仿佛所有人都被迫放下了手头的事情。那当然不是事实。从一些方面来看，它并非一次显著的震动。美国音乐产业的某些部分仍维持原样，与我在上一章所提及的无异。Phil Spector给the Righteous Brothers制作了一首热门单曲，即1964年的《You‘ve Lost that Lovin’ Feelin'》。 若追溯Motown唱片在整个60年代的发展过程，你会发现它在64年实现了质的飞跃，几乎正是the Beatles在美国初次亮相之同时。举个例子，若追查1964年到1966年间the Beatles和the Supremes两者各自的单曲何时走红，你会发现the Supremes真的就是紧随the Beatles之后。她们正是一个女子组合，除此之外你还能给the Supremes下别的定义吗？我原以为英伦入侵挤占了女子组合的生存空间，但这种挤占其实是比较有限的。这个组合来自底特律，而非纽约，但说到底她们还是一个女子组合。所以这其中包含了一种连续性。不过，the Beatles和英伦入侵确实震动了这门产业。而到1965年夏天，美国乐队又回到了大众视线之中。这次会是民谣摇滚，是Bob Dylan和the Byrds；还有来自南加利福尼亚的新声音，其得到了音乐产业的关注。这就是我们会在下一章讲到的，美国人对于英伦入侵的回应。
body.en:
Speaking of Beatles-type or Rolling Stones–type bands, two really cannot be simply slotted into either. They are the Kinks and the Who. In the period we are covering—1964 to 1966—both had great success in Britain. The Kinks also scored some results in America, but the Who’s cold reception there is striking; only a few songs became lasting U.S. singles. I will not jump ahead and scramble the plan.

One reason the Kinks and the Who are hard to classify is that both are known for forceful, aggressive music. That makes them look a bit like the Rolling Stones—blues influence, power, guitar-led playing. Yet beyond forceful music, both show intelligence. Their lyrics are thoughtful, closer to real songwriter craft—more like the Beatles’ Lennon–McCartney pairing than Mick Jagger and Keith Richards. So the Kinks and the Who fuse the two big bands’ styles. Their main writers—Ray Davies of the Kinks, Pete Townshend of the Who—push strong musical means and blend both bands’ traits into styles of their own, hard to label Beatles-type or Stones-type.

As I said, neither made the huge U.S. splash of the Beatles or the Stones. The Kinks did better on singles, but hit a snag on the road to bigger success: somehow they were barred from entering the U.S. I think their behavior was too wild, and immigration would not reissue visas. Unable to revisit America and promote in person, record sales struggled. The Who had little success until 1967’s “I Can See for Miles” reached No. 9—a modest breakthrough. Their real U.S. breakthrough starts with Tommy, outside this chapter’s scope. We will mention it with psychedelic music: Tommy, 1969.

When I think of the Kinks’ work I think of songs like “You Really Got Me.” In 1964 it hit No. 1 in Britain and No. 7 in America. Very hard, aggressive; it opens with a guitar lick that may owe a little to “Louie Louie.” In the late 1970s Van Halen covered “You Really Got Me.” “All Day and All of the Night”—if you play guitar, it looks very like “You Really Got Me.” Slightly change the fingering for “You Really Got Me” and you can play “All Day and All of the Night.” That is the craftsman’s view: the band found the approach worked on “You Really Got Me,” tweaked it, and with “All Day and All of the Night” delivered almost the same thing. Common in the pop business. First song topped Britain; the second hit No. 2. Both hits. In 1964 the second also reached No. 7 in the U.S. “Tired of Waiting for You” uses a similar chord path to those two, but arpeggiated, so the likeness is less obvious. In 1965 it hit No. 1 Britain and No. 6 America. “Till the End of the Day” keeps traits of the above; No. 6 Britain in 1965, no U.S. chart. Ray Davies meant to keep writing that way, but John Lennon’s lyrics grew more philosophical, and Dylan became a major performer in summer 1965, so Davies’s lyrics grew more philosophical too—reflecting on society, discontent with the status quo. “A Well Respected Man” is a good example: criticizing conformity and dull expectations, people wearing masks, never showing true character; they should show the real self and be sincere. That critical streak you can hear in Bob Dylan’s “Ballad of a Thin Man” or John Lennon’s “Nowhere Man”—and now add Ray Davies.

Now turn to the Who. In many ways the band is a collection of interesting characters. Pete Townshend, guitarist, outstanding songwriter—writes the songs and the overall concepts. But he only sings part of the time—harmonies, occasional lead. Singing is mainly Roger Daltrey’s job. He is a bit like the role Robert Plant later played in the late 1960s and 1970s—the sexy frontman who just sings the tunes. In many ways also like Mick Jagger or Elvis. Then wild drummer Keith Moon and seasoned bassist John Entwistle. Among these four you hear a powerful trio-plus-voice releasing forceful music, with increasingly complex lyrics and concepts behind it. The Who hit we first think of is “My Generation.” In 1965 it reached No. 2 in Britain, but many are surprised it did not catch on in America that year. In fact it never entered the U.S. charts. We often feel it did because the Who’s 1970s success put those early-1960s singles into heavy radio rotation. Now they sit in classic-rock playlists, so they seem as if they were always hits. “My Generation” was not, then. Nor was “I Can’t Explain,” another we often hear—No. 8 Britain in 1965, not a U.S. hit. “Substitute,” another important 1965 song, reached No. 2 in Britain with no U.S. splash. As I said, “I Can See for Miles” was a breakthrough, but that was already 1967. And the big breakthrough was 1969’s Tommy.

The Who were also part of a British movement almost unrelated to America: the Mods. If you have seen Quadrophenia you know something of it—Sting is in that film. It is interesting: a cinematic take on the Who’s concept album Quadrophenia. Set at Brighton beach, where two groups of young people with different values staged a famous clash. Rockers wore leather, greased ducktails, chains, big Harley bikes. Mods were neat, clean, preferred Vespa scooters to big bikes—a bit dandyish. One weekend the two met at Brighton and fought. City-wide disturbance; papers full of Mods vs Rockers. In the end the Who became the representative band Mods chose. America never really had a Mods movement, but Mods liked Motown records, danced a lot, and treated the Who almost as idols—part of Mod culture. In Britain that Mod/Rocker opposition also appears in the Beatles’ A Hard Day’s Night. Somewhere the band faces a string of questions. Someone asks John how he found America; Lennon says turn left at Greenland. Someone asks Ringo if he is a Mod or a Rocker—referring to Brighton. He says neither—I’m a Mocker. Of course in 1964 America no one knew what they meant. It sounded funny; for Britons who knew the pop culture of the moment, the meaning was immediate. So the Who were tightly linked to the Mods, and that link helped British chart success. Without a Mod movement in America, their music never really broke through there.

All right—we have covered the Kinks and the Who. Time to review what this whole chapter covered. The British Invasion opened new opportunities for British artists. Not only at home: for America, these new faces also shook the U.S. music industry. In fact we had seen something similar. From 1955 to 1957, independent-label records crossed over onto mainstream pop charts and pushed major-label product to the margins. Majors rushed out similar records. People were surprised; we also saw how it ended. Payola scandals in 1959–60; industry giants regained control. In early 1964 a similar pattern returned in America. The Beatles and other British artists arrived and scored huge success. A new threat—so the common story is that the Invasion completely shook the U.S. industry, as if everyone had to drop what they were doing. That of course is not true. In some respects it was not a dramatic shock. Parts of the American industry stayed as I described last chapter. Phil Spector produced a hit for the Righteous Brothers in 1964—“You’ve Lost That Lovin’ Feelin’.” Trace Motown through the 1960s and you see a qualitative leap in 1964, almost exactly when the Beatles first appeared in America. For example, track when Beatles and Supremes singles hit from 1964 to 1966 and you find the Supremes really following right after the Beatles. They are a girl group—what else can you call the Supremes? I once thought the Invasion squeezed girl groups out, but the squeeze was fairly limited. This group was from Detroit, not New York, but they were still a girl group. So there is continuity. Still, the Beatles and the Invasion did shake the business. By summer 1965 American bands were back in public view—folk-rock, Bob Dylan and the Byrds, and new sounds from Southern California that the industry noticed. That is what the next chapter covers: America’s reply to the British Invasion.
